meta.title: Checkpoint: Filling In the Chord
meta.summary: Three notes across five windows — which forms hold whole, which live as fragments, and where the third is hiding in each one.

prompt.text: Which forms are worth holding as a
barre? Select every one that is.

spans.text: The C form
The A form
The G form
The E form
The D form

explanation.text: Two of the five, and they are the two barre chords almost everyone already owns. Neither asks for more than two frets past the barre. The C form strands its root three frets out, the G form spans four frets with the little finger on two strings that aren't adjacent, and the D form only ever had four strings to begin with — those three live as two- and three-string fragments, and that is the normal case rather than a concession. Treating all five as barre chords you simply haven't mastered yet is the fastest way to give up on CAGED.

prompt.text: The E form barre sounds all six strings, but a C major triad is only three notes. Which describes what those six strings are actually holding?

spans.text: Six different notes — that's what makes a barre chord sound fuller than a triad.
Three roots, two fifths and one third — so the only
is on string 3, and the chord's whole quality rests on it.
Two roots, two thirds and two fifths — each note of the triad doubled once.
Three roots, two thirds and one fifth — the same arrangement as the G form.

explanation.text: The A form's window runs frets 2–6 and the G form's runs 4–8, so they share frets 4–6 — and the three dots living there are
